Evaluating AI Where It Is Hardest: Low-Resource Languages
The most consequential gap in artificial intelligence today is not capability — it is coverage. Frontier models perform impressively in English and a handful of high-resource languages, then degrade sharply in the languages spoken by the communities that global impact organisations exist to serve. Vendor benchmarks rarely surface this decline, because they are seldom designed to look for it.

Gooey.AI was built to close that measurement gap. Because our platform aggregates both leading private models — OpenAI, Google, Anthropic — and the strongest open-weight alternatives from India, Europe and China, including Mistral, SwissAI, Qwen, Kimi and DeepSeek, we can benchmark competing model families on an identical task, in an identical language, against an identical rubric. Our public low-resource language evaluation work is published at gooey.ai/language, with domain-specific agricultural advisory evaluation at gooey.ai/ageval.

What distinguishes this approach is the unit of analysis. We evaluate the AI workflow — a human-readable chain of prompts, abstracted model calls, retrieval documents and tool calls, paired with use-case-specific "golden" input and output datasets — rather than an abstract model score. A model that leads a general leaderboard may fail badly at Swahili agricultural advice delivered over SMS. Evaluating at workflow level produces findings that translate directly into deployment decisions: which model, in which language, for which use case, at what cost, and under which sovereignty constraints.

This work is grounded in deployment rather than laboratory conditions. Gooey.AI supports over 1,500 languages and has served 1.5 million users through WhatsApp, Telegram, SMS, voice and web — the channels frontline communities actually use. We conduct low-resource language and agricultural evaluations on behalf of the Gates Foundation, where we also sit on its AI Advisory Committee for Agriculture and Digital Public Infrastructure.

Every prompt, model version, corpus and cost remains transparent and reproducible. Our orchestration platform is Apache 2.0 licensed and in certification as a Digital Public Good — because claims about language performance should be verifiable by anyone, not asserted by the vendor.

prompt: Write a 300 word essay on Gooey's sovereign stack
output:
Here's a standalone 300-word essay.

The Sovereign Stack: AI That Stays Where It Belongs
For a growing number of institutions, the decisive question about an AI system is no longer how good is it? but where does it run, and who can switch it off? Ministries, universities and impact organisations across the Global South and Europe increasingly share a concern: they do not want their data, or their inference spending, leaving their borders — and they do not want a change in geopolitics to sever access to tools their frontline services now depend on.

Gooey.AI treats sovereignty as an architectural property rather than a compliance checkbox. The foundation is abstraction. We reduce AI systems to workflows — human-readable chains of prompts, abstracted model calls, retrieval documents and tool calls — so that the model itself becomes a swappable component. An organisation can run a workflow on OpenAI, Google or Anthropic today, and on Mistral, SwissAI, Qwen, Kimi or DeepSeek tomorrow, without rewriting the application. Hot-swappability is what makes independence real: no vendor lock-in, and a genuine option to select whichever model is faster, cheaper, cleaner or more sovereign this month.

The second layer is deployment. Alongside standard certifications — HIPAA, GDPR and SOC 2 Type II — we offer in-country, on-premise and airgapped server support, so that inference and data can remain within national jurisdiction where policy or law requires it.

The third layer is openness. Our orchestration platform is Apache 2.0 licensed and currently in certification as a Digital Public Good with the Digital Public Goods Alliance. Open source is the ultimate sovereignty guarantee: an institution that holds the code cannot be locked out of it.

Underpinning all three is radical transparency. Every prompt, model, retrieval database and cost is visible. Sovereignty, in the end, is not a promise a vendor makes — it is a property a customer can inspect, verify and, if necessary, exercise without permission.

Low-Code as a Distribution Strategy
The scarcest resource in global impact work is not ambition — it is engineering capacity. The programme manager who understands exactly what her 10,000 frontline health workers need is rarely the person who can build it, and the queue for the organisation's two developers is measured in quarters. AI's promise stalls in that queue.

Gooey.AI's low-code approach removes it. Our platform lowers the barrier far enough that non-coders can vibe-code working agents — moving from intent to a testable, deployed prototype without waiting for an engineering sprint. The mechanism is the AI workflow: a small, human-readable chain of prompts, abstracted model calls, retrieval documents and tool calls, assembled and edited in plain language rather than code. Because a workflow is a small artefact rather than a codebase, it can be read, understood, forked and improved by someone who has never written a function.

That legibility has a second effect: it makes AI spreadable. Workflows are shared in collaborative workspaces, where teams see one another's work and can discover and fork the workflows of other organisations in their field. A proven approach in Kenyan agriculture becomes a starting point in Indian education, without a rebuild. This is why we treat low-code not merely as a usability feature but as a distribution strategy for innovation.

Deployment matters just as much as authoring. A workflow can ship instantly to the channels the Global South actually uses — WhatsApp, Telegram, Facebook, SMS, voice and web — so usability testing happens with real users, in real languages, in days rather than months. Built-in evaluation and impact dashboards then show whether it is working.

The result reframes who gets to build. Professors, programme managers, tech leads and students all become authors rather than petitioners — and product-market fit is discovered in the field, by the people closest to the problem.

Orchestration as the Layer That Sets You Free
Most organisations do not have a model problem. They have an orchestration problem. Choosing a model is a single decision; wiring prompts, retrieval, tool calls, channels, analytics and billing around that model is a permanent commitment — and it is that surrounding machinery, not the model, that quietly locks a customer in. Rip out the vendor and the whole assembly comes with it.

Gooey.AI inverts that relationship. We abstract everything into AI workflow recipes: small, collaborative artefacts combining LLM prompts, chained model calls, tool calls and code snippets, RAG documents, analytics, and use-case-specific golden evaluation datasets. The model is a parameter inside the recipe, not the foundation beneath it. Swap it and the workflow keeps running.

That abstraction makes genuine vendor-agnosticism practical rather than theoretical. Our platform aggregates the best private models — OpenAI, Google, Anthropic — alongside the strongest open-weight alternatives from India, Europe and China, including Mistral, SwissAI, Qwen, Kimi and DeepSeek. Because each workflow carries its own golden eval dataset, switching is an evidence-based decision: run the same task against a new model, compare results on the use case that actually matters, and adopt whichever is smarter, faster, cheaper, cleaner or more sovereign this month. Hot-swappability without evaluation is just churn; paired with evals, it becomes compounding advantage.

The operational layer follows the same logic. One organisational billing account spans every private and public model, so procurement does not have to be renegotiated each time the frontier moves. Every prompt, model, retrieval database and cost stays visible.

The strategic ambition is larger. By pushing open source and abstraction, we intend workflows to become a new layer that commoditises the models beneath them — and, through our open-source vision and AI workflow standards work, to commoditise the runtime itself, for customers' benefit rather than ours.

Proving It: Measurement as a First-Class Feature
Global impact work has a long history of expensive pilots that were never honestly assessed. AI has made the problem worse, not better: it is now trivially easy to ship something that looks impressive in a demo and impossible, six months later, to say whether it changed an outcome for anyone. Budgets are tightening precisely as the temptation to spend on AI intensifies. Measurement is what separates the two.

Gooey.AI treats monitoring and evaluation as part of the product rather than a reporting obligation bolted on afterwards. Every workflow ships with built-in dashboards covering impact, usage and NPS, so the questions a funder will eventually ask — who used this, how often, did it help, would they recommend it — are answerable from day one rather than reconstructed retrospectively.

The deeper mechanism is the golden evaluation dataset. Each workflow recipe carries use-case-specific desirable inputs and outputs, defined with partner organisations who bring grounded scenarios from the field. This turns quality from an opinion into a test. It also makes progress cumulative: when a new model is released, the question is not whether it tops a general leaderboard but whether it improves this metric, on this task, in this language. Constant AI advances become measurable business improvement rather than undirected churn.

We also make evaluation legible to non-specialists. Use-case-based evals and ROI dashboards can be structured around an organisation's own Theory of Change, so results speak in the language of the mission rather than the language of machine learning. Radical transparency completes the picture: every prompt, model, retrieval database and cost is visible, so cost-per-outcome is calculable, not estimated.

The effect is a faster, more honest loop — prototype, test with real users, measure, iterate — which is how 1.5 million users and over 2,200 paying clients found workflows that actually work.

Beyond Bias: Asking Whose World the Model Imagines
Ask a generative image model for "a doctor," "a wedding," or "a family," and it will answer with striking confidence — and a narrow imagination. The output will reflect the distribution of its training data, which is to say the distribution of who has historically been photographed, published and captioned online. For a Global South audience, the result is a machine that renders their world as an exception rather than a default. This is not a bug to be patched. It is a question about who participates in building the systems.

Beyond Bias, a collaboration between Gooey.AI and Goethe-Institut India launched in March 2025, takes that question seriously. Rather than treating bias as a technical parameter to be tuned by engineers, the initiative reimagines generative AI through participatory practice — bringing artists, designers, students and cultural practitioners into direct contact with the models, and asking them to interrogate how gender, caste and race are represented in what those models produce.

The method is deliberately hands-on. Through public prompt-a-thons and workshops held in Bangalore, Delhi and beyond, participants probe model behaviour, document what they find, and contribute toward more inclusive datasets and tools. The output is not only critique but artefact: shared workflows, evidence and creative work that others can examine and build on. The initiative's approach has since been documented in a research paper on participatory and reflective approaches to cultural AI.

For Gooey.AI, Beyond Bias sits naturally alongside our low-resource language evaluation work. Both proceed from the same conviction — that the performance of AI in underrepresented contexts must be examined empirically, by the people affected, rather than assumed from a vendor's benchmark. And both establish a foothold in a market we intend to serve seriously: cultural institutions, museums and universities navigating what AI means for art, heritage and creative control.

Open Source as Trust Infrastructure

They need to know what they can inspect, what they can keep, and what happens if the vendor changes its mind.

Gooey.AI's answer is unambiguous. Openness at Gooey operates at three levels. The first is the codebase — inspectable, deployable and forkable, which means an organisation that adopts us cannot be locked out of what it has built. The second is the workflow. Because recipes are small, human-readable artefacts rather than opaque applications, they are legible to non-engineers and shareable by design. Collaborative workspaces let teams see one another's work and discover and fork workflows from other organisations in their field — so a solution proven in one context becomes a starting point in another rather than a rebuild. The third is radical transparency in operation: every prompt, model, retrieval database and cost is visible. Nothing about how an answer was produced, or what it cost, is hidden behind an abstraction we control.

The strategic intent behind this is deliberate. Through our open-source vision and AI workflow standards work, we want the workflow layer — and ultimately the runtime itself — to become commoditised, for customers' benefit rather than ours.

Agriculture: Where the Hardest AI Problems Live
A smallholder farmer with two acres notices something wrong with her crop. She has a question, a feature phone, patchy connectivity, and a language that appears nowhere near the top of any model leaderboard. She needs an answer this week, not next season, and a confidently wrong one may cost her the harvest.

Every difficult problem in applied AI converges on that moment: low-resource language performance, low-bandwidth delivery, real economic stakes, and no tolerance for hallucination. It is why Gooey.AI chose agriculture as the field in which to prove the platform first.

We serve as the AI middleware provider and partner for Farmer.chat, a multilingual WhatsApp bot for smallholder farmers across India and Africa, which was demonstrated at the UN General Assembly Science Panel. We are also the AI platform behind Opportunity.org and Safaricom's DigiFarm in Kenya — deployments that reach farmers through the channels they already use rather than an app they must be persuaded to install.

Rigour matters as much as reach. Our agricultural advisory evaluation work is published at gooey.ai/ageval, built on golden evaluation datasets developed with partner organisations who supply grounded, real-world scenarios. This means model selection is settled by evidence on the actual task — is this advice correct, in this language, for this crop and region — rather than by general benchmark scores.

That work has earned a seat at the table. Gooey.AI sits on the Gates Foundation's AI Advisory Committee for Agriculture and Digital Public Infrastructure, and conducts low-resource language and agricultural advisory evaluations on the Foundation's behalf.

Agriculture was deliberately our beachhead: develop excellent public workflows with partners in one field, prove resonance and monetisation, then extend the pattern. The method it taught us — grounded evals, local languages, frontline channels — is what we now carry into health and education.

Health and Education: Extending the Pattern
Agriculture taught us a method rather than a domain: build excellent public workflows with partners who bring grounded scenarios, evaluate against golden datasets in the languages that matter, ship to the channels people already use, and measure whether anything actually improved. Health and education are where that method travels next.

In health, we are the AI platform provider — alongside Google — for the Wellcome Trust's Mental Health Accelerator. Mental health is an unforgiving test case. Advice must be safe, culturally legible and delivered in the user's own language, often through a phone rather than a clinic. It is precisely the kind of problem where a general benchmark score tells you almost nothing and a use-case-specific evaluation tells you everything. After our work in agriculture, global health is the logical field for deeper engagement, and one of the markets we intend to serve seriously.

In education, TeachForIndia is a live deployment under the Rockefeller Foundation's AI Workflow Accelerator, sitting alongside implementations at the UN Office of Immigration and the City of Seattle's non-emergency helpline. The accelerator model matters here: rather than building one bespoke system, partners create workflows others in their field can find, fork and adapt.

Universities represent the other half of the education story, and a different set of needs. Professors want to bring advanced AI tools to their students; IT heads want a simple, fixed-cost option that avoids on-premise complexity; students arrive because their institution grants them credits, and can buy more if they want to keep building. Our model-agnosticism, sovereign deployment options and cultural work make us a credible answer to all three.

The connective thread is the workflow itself — small, legible, forkable. A pattern proven with farmers in Kenya becomes a starting point for a teacher in Delhi, without a rebuild.
